Fortunatus
for-tyoo-NAH-tus
proper noun (figure)
Latin Fortunatus ("blessed, fortunate, prospered"), from fortuna ("fortune"). A common Roman name, often borne by slaves and freedmen. One of three Corinthian believers who refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Cor 16:17).

Biblical Definition

Fortunatus was a Christian at Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Achaicus, came to the Apostle Paul (likely at Ephesus, bringing the letter and gifts of the Corinthian church) and refreshed his spirit during a difficult season of ministry. Paul writes: "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:17-18). Of Fortunatus himself we know only his name and this one service, but the service was real and valued: in supplying "that which was lacking" from the Corinthians (perhaps practical support, perhaps simply their presence and fellowship), these three men ministered to the apostle's weary spirit. The phrase "they have refreshed my spirit" is precious: even the great apostle, who poured himself out for the churches, needed and received refreshment from ordinary believers. His Latin name, common among the servile classes, again suggests a man of humble origin, perhaps a slave or freedman, whose service to the apostle was nonetheless recorded forever in the inspired Word. Fortunatus models the ministry of refreshment — the often-overlooked grace of being a refreshment to weary servants of Christ. Paul elsewhere prays for the household of Onesiphorus because "he oft refreshed me" (2 Tim 1:16), and the writer to Philemon rejoices that "the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee" (Philem 7). To refresh the spirit of a weary laborer is a real and commendable ministry, and Fortunatus is forever named among those who did it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Corinthian believer who, with Stephanas and Achaicus, came to Paul and "refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Cor 16:17-18); his Latin name ("blessed") suggests humble origin; the model of the ministry of refreshment to weary servants of Christ.

FORTUNATUS, proper noun. Latin Fortunatus ("blessed, fortunate"); a common Roman name, often of slaves and freedmen.

A Christian of Corinth, named once: 1 Cor 16:17, with Stephanas and Achaicus.

The three came to Paul, supplied "that which was lacking," and refreshed his spirit (1 Cor 16:17-18).

His humble name suggests servile origin; his service to the apostle was recorded forever in Scripture.

The model of the ministry of refreshment to weary servants of Christ (cf. Onesiphorus, 2 Tim 1:16; Philem 7).

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 16:17-18 — "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such."

2 Timothy 1:16 — "The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain."

Philemon 1:7 — "For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother."

Proverbs 25:13 — "As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters."

Modern Corruption

Fortunatus is corrupted only when the ministry of refreshment is undervalued — when the church forgets that even the strongest servants of Christ need refreshing, and that to be a refreshment to the weary is a real and recorded grace.

expand to see more

Refreshment-undervalued. The ministry of Fortunatus was simple: he, with two others, came to Paul and refreshed his spirit. In a results-obsessed church culture that prizes visible achievement, the grace of merely refreshing a weary laborer can seem too small to notice. Scripture notices it. Paul names Fortunatus forever for this service; he prays mercy on Onesiphorus's house because "he oft refreshed me" (2 Tim 1:16); Philemon is praised because the saints' hearts are refreshed by him (Philem 7). The faithful messenger refreshes the soul of those who send him "as the cold of snow in the time of harvest" (Prov 25:13). To refresh the weary is a ministry the Lord records and rewards.

Fortunatus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the value Scripture places on the ministry of refreshment. Even the great apostle, pouring himself out for the churches, needed refreshment and received it from ordinary believers of humble name. The church that learns from Fortunatus learns to honor and to practice the grace of refreshing weary servants of Christ — pastors, missionaries, and laborers who, like Paul, need the cold of snow in the time of harvest.
